## Today's Goals {.smaller}

Today we will

- Model Assessment and Selection

We will use the CRU **and** FAO data

- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/CRU/parquet`
  - Filter to annual data
- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/FAO/parquet`
  - Filter to Avocado Yields
- Join on `Year` and `ISO3` into a single dataset




  
## Loading Datasets

First load the CRU and FAO data from Parquet Files

```{r load_fao}
#| echo: true
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
# Load the full fao dataset
read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"FAO","parquet","FAO_crop_livestock.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Item == "Avocados" & Element == "Yield") -> faostat_avocado

read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"CRU","parquet","tmp_w_ISO3.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Period == "ANN") -> cru_tmp_ann

faostat_avocado |>
  inner_join(cru_tmp_ann,join_by(ISO3,Year),suffix=c("_fao","_cru")) |>
  drop_na(ISO3) -> avocado_tmp
```

## Propose a model

From our visual analysis

- There may be a relationship between temperature and yields
- Propose the linear model

$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 Temperature + \epsilon$$

## Train an OLS Model using data from Mexico

```{r train-mexico-model}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 == "MEX") -> avocado_tmp_mex

lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru,
  data=avocado_tmp_mex
) -> yield_model

print(yield_model)
```


## Apply this model to forecast yields in Columbia

```{r forecast-columbia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(moderndive)
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 == "COL") -> avocado_tmp_col

get_regression_points(
  yield_model, newdata=avocado_tmp_col
) -> predicted_yield_col

print(predicted_yield_col)
```

## Visualize model predictions

```{r viz-pred-columbia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(predicted_yield_col) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat),color="black",size=1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="Modeled Yields for Columbia",
    x="Actual Yield",
    y="Predicted Yield"
  )
```


## Model Assessment

Does this model do a good job predicting yields in Columbia?

- Systematically over-predicts yields (inaccurate)
- High variability in predictions (imprecise)
- Model seems to make very poor predictions
- Why?
- What can we do?

# Multivariate Modeling

## Why Multivariate Models

- Likely more than one factor impacts yields
  - Temperature, precipitation, technology, etc
- Modeling yield as only a function of temperature gives poor results
  - Ignores other important factors
  - May confuse other factors with temperature effects
- Leads to multivariate modeling

## Multivariate Models

Multivariate models include multiple features
$$y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n + \epsilon$$

- Simultaneously account for each feature ($x_1$ to $x_n$)
- Each parameter ($b_1$ to $b_n$) represents
  - Effect of the associated feature on the label
  - Holding all other features constant


## Multivariate Models in R

How do we implement multivariate models in R?

. . .

- Add additional features to the formula
- Separate features using the `+` operator
- **Interact** features using the `*` operator
- Create factors using the `factor()` function


# Implementing Multivariate Models

## Controlling for technological Progress

We modeled yields as a function of temperature

- Average temperatures are increasing over time
- Technology is improving over time
- Ignoring technology improvements would
  - Cause the model to attribute technological improvements to temperature
  - Overstate the impact of temperature on yields
- How can we account for technological progress?

## Accounting for technological progress

We can account for technological progress by

- Directly including features that measure the impact of technology on yields
- Constructing a **proxy** for technological advancement
  - We know yields have steadily been rising over time
  - We could include time as a feature in our model
  
## Using time as a proxy for technology

We can train the model
$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 \cdot Temperature + b_2 \cdot Year + \epsilon$$

What does this function imply?

- Yields rise linearly with time due to technology
  - **Holding temperature constant**
- Yields rise linearly with temperature 
  - **Holding technology constant**
  
Train this model. What do we get?


## Controlling for Technology

```{r model-technology}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru + Year,
  data=avocado_tmp_mex
) -> yield_model_tech

print(yield_model_tech)
```
```{r get-params}
b0 = format(coefficients(yield_model_tech)[["(Intercept)"]],scientific=FALSE,digits=4)
b1 = format(coefficients(yield_model_tech)[["Value_cru"]],scientific=FALSE,digits=4)
b2 = format(coefficients(yield_model_tech)[["Year"]],scientific=FALSE,digits=4)
```
$$Yield = `r b0` + `r b1` \cdot Temp + `r b2` \cdot Yr$$
Is this model "better" than our previous model? How can we tell?


## Visualize Model Predictions

Visualize predictions against the actual values
```{r viz-predictions-tech}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_points(yield_model_tech) -> points_tech

ggplot(points_tech) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat),color="black",size=1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="Modeled Yields for Mexico",
    subtitle="Controling for Temperature and Technology",
    x="Actual Yield",
    y="Predicted Yield"
  )
```

## Compare Across Models

```{r viz-predictions-tech-2}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_points(yield_model) -> points_tmp

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data=points_tmp,aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat,color="Temp Only"),size=2.5) +
  geom_point(data=points_tech,aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat,color="Temp+Tech"),size=2.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="Modeled Yields for Mexico",
    x="Actual Yield",
    y="Predicted Yield",
    color="Model"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Temp Only" = "blue","Temp+Tech" = "black"))
```
Which model is better?


# Evaluating Models

## Numerically evaluating models

Graphical evaluations of models are useful but limited

- Quickly give a sense of accuracy, precision, and potential pitfalls
- Comparisons won't always be definitive
- We'd prefer a numeric measure of model performance
- Do we already have one?

## Measures of model fit/performance

- OLS uses MSE as its **loss function**
  - A single number that evaluates prediction errors on the training data
  - Zero means a "perfect" model
  - Larger numbers mean predictions are less "good"
- OLS chooses the model parameters that **mathematically minimize the loss function**
  - No other choice of parameters can reduce the MSE
- We would tend to prefer models with lower MSE
- MSE is not the only metric for model performance

## Computing model performance metrics

Get model performance metrics with `get_regression_summaries()`
```{r model-summaries}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_summaries(yield_model)
get_regression_summaries(yield_model_tech)
```

## Model performance metrics

The computed metrics are

- **r_squared** - The [R-Squared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_determination) Statistic
  - Squared correlation between model predictions and actual values
  - Ranges from 0 to 1
  - Values close to 1 mean predictions more strongly correlated with actual values
- In OLS adding features will **always reduce the R-squared**!
  - Regardless of whether the feature is "relevant"
  
## Model performance metrics

The computed metrics are

- **adj_r_squared** - The [Adjusted R-Squared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_determination#Adjusted_R2)
  - The R-squared, reduced by a factor related to the number of model features
  - Typically ranges from 0 to 1, but can be negative
  - Values close to 1 mean predictions strongly correlated with actual values
- In OLS adding features may increase or decrease the Adjusted R-Squared
  - The penalty scales with features/observations

  
## Model performance metrics

The computed metrics are

- **mse** - The Mean Squared Error
  - The loss function in OLS
  - Values close to zero mean predictions are close to actual values
- In OLS adding features will **always reduce the MSE**
  - Regardless of whether the feature is "relevant"
- **rmse** is the square root of MSE

## Model performance metrics

The other metrics

- **sigma** - Variance of the model residual
- **statistic** - The statistic from an [F-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-test) that all parameters
(excluding the intercept) are zero
- **p-value** - The p-value of the above F-test
- **df** - The Model [Degrees of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degrees_of_freedom_(statistics)) from the above F-test
- **nobs** - The number of observations in the training data

## Evaluating Models {.smaller}

Which model do you prefer and why?

$Yield = b_0 + b_1 \cdot Temp$
```{r}
#| echo: false
get_regression_summaries(yield_model,print=TRUE)
```

$Yield = b_0 + b_1 \cdot Temp + b_2 \cdot Yr$
```{r}
#| echo: false
get_regression_summaries(yield_model_tech,print=TRUE)
```
